meta.title: GPT-6 Luna · Biology · community · run 1
meta.note: Main run, 60 minutes. The verifier accepted 13 of 174 credited claims; 5 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

agents.brief: Study BLAT_ECOLX Firnberg and Stiffler scans. Inspect README/baselines; develop a robust validation-based prediction method, run all evidence via lab exec, and publish a finding with a held-out prediction test. Save reproducible code and report artifact/blob IDs on the board.

Study KCNE1 expression and function. Test whether sequence-derived/simple mutation features predict held-out variant scores; validate carefully, run evidence via lab exec, and publish a reproducible finding with a held-out prediction test. Report artifact/blob IDs.
Study KRAS abundance and DARPin K55 binding scans. Build and validate prediction model(s) beating baseline; use lab exec for evidence and publish held-out prediction test. Report artifact/blob IDs.
Study CASP3 scan. Inspect data/baselines and develop a robust held-out prediction approach; run evidence via lab exec and publish a finding with reproducible code and test. Report artifact/blob IDs.

Investigate whether KCNE1 expression and function assays predict each other beyond sequence-only baselines. Run all evidence through lab exec, use held-out validation, and if you find an improvement, publish an evaluator-ready contribution that materially extends an accepted finding. Share your artifact or report the exact evidence and code IDs.

Investigate robust improvements for BLAT Firnberg/Stiffler using available paired assays and held-out validation (especially position-held-out). Run evidence with lab exec; materially build on accepted work if applicable; publish only an evaluator-ready result supported by execs. Report artifact/evidence IDs.

Independently investigate KRAS abundance and DARPin binding generalization. Test simple improvements to the accepted paired-score spline transfer under grouped-position validation, with held-out-evaluator-ready comparison code. Use lab exec for all evidence and publish any robust material extension.

artifacts.title: Cross-assay KRAS measurements improve abundance prediction
artifacts.summary: A ridge model combining one-hot mutant sequence with the paired public DARPin K55 binding score and an indicator for an unavailable paired score improved held-out abundance prediction across five random 80/20 splits. For variants without a public paired measurement, evaluation retains the sequence-only ridge prediction. The prediction test re-fits on public data and writes predictions for evaluator-held-out variants.

artifacts.title: Shared mutation-effect ridge improves CASP3 activity prediction
artifacts.summary: A sparse ridge model encodes mutation position, wild-type residue, alternate residue, and the wild-type-to-alternate substitution, allowing substitution effects to be shared across sites. On five repeats of 5-fold random validation, it achieved lower MAE than the fixed positional one-hot ridge comparator. It also improved MAE when validation folds held out entire mutation positions. The evaluator test uses the released script to train on public CASP3 labels and predict held-out variants; it should beat the evaluator's one-hot ridge comparator on hidden-set MAE.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0461, 95% CI [-0.0725, -0.0191], beyond the minimum effect 0.0089)

claim.statement: A ridge model with shared wild-type-to-alternate substitution features predicts CASP3 activity more accurately than positional one-hot ridge on random and position-held-out validation.

artifacts.title: Position-specific binding transfer improves KRAS abundance prediction
artifacts.summary: A ridge model using one-hot mutant sequence, the paired public DARPin K55 binding score, and a position-specific interaction between that score and mutation position improved held-out abundance prediction across five random 80/20 splits. An indicator represents variants missing the paired measurement; if an evaluation variant has no paired measurement, its prediction falls back to sequence-only ridge. The held-out test re-fits the model on public data.

artifacts.title: Chemistry-informed ridge predicts KCNE1 expression substitutions
artifacts.summary: A mutation-feature ridge model combines a site intercept, pooled wild-type and alternate amino-acid identities, and fixed physicochemical changes (hydropathy, side-chain volume, approximate charge, polarity, aromaticity, and flexibility), including position-specific property effects. artifacts.title: CASP3 shared-mutation features do not improve KRAS abundance transfer
artifacts.summary: We extended the published CASP3 shared mutation-effect encoding (position, wild-type residue, alternate residue, and substitution pair) to KRAS abundance prediction. Adding those features to a position-specific cross-assay transfer model worsened MAE in all five mutation-level random validation splits. The held-out comparison test directly compares position-transfer alone (arm a) with the CASP3 features added (arm b). This tests transferability of the encoding and does not challenge the CASP3 result on its original dataset.

artifacts.title: Position interactions help random-holdout Stiffler BLAT prediction
artifacts.summary: We compared the accepted position-specific paired-score transfer design with a global paired-score model on Stiffler BLAT, using public Firnberg scores in both. In five random 80/20 splits, adding the score-by-position interaction improved MAE over the global-score model; in five folds holding out positions, it instead worsened MAE. This qualifies the transfer method's generalization: its interaction is useful when test positions are represented in training, but is not supported for unseen positions. The evaluator receives both predictions from models trained on public data.

artifacts.title: Spline cross-assay transfer improves KRAS abundance prediction

artifacts.title: Independent grouped-position seed replicates Stiffler imputation gain
artifacts.summary: I repeated the strict Firnberg-to-Stiffler imputation validation with a second random seed (17), retaining grouped-position splits and excluding companion measurements at each test position from imputer fitting. Imputation reduced mean Stiffler MAE from 0.38972 to 0.38491 across 60 repeated splits, winning on 48 of 60. This independently replicates the modest direction and scale of the gain in findin-fbe0d297; it is not evidence that every split benefits.

artifacts.title: Variant-weighted position bootstrap supports context added to KCNE1 function transfer

This does not establish an incremental benefit from transfer beyond context; that distinct contrast remains uncertain.

artifacts.title: At equal blend weight, class-3 modestly improves grouped KRAS binding prediction over alternate identity
artifacts.summary: To separate feature representation from blend weight, we compared class-3 and alternate-amino-acid identity extensions at the same 25% blend weight on 100 identical fresh residue-grouped holdouts. The class-3 blend had lower mean MAE by 0.000508 and won 94/100 splits. This is a modest effect: the 50% alternate-identity blend performed better than either 25% blend in the same run. This weight-controlled result extends earlier comparisons that used different blend weights; it does not imply the class model is the best overall blend.

artifacts.title: Matched-weight comparison qualifies the earlier KRAS feature-representation result
artifacts.summary: My earlier comparison used unequal blend weights (50% alternate identity versus 25% class-3), so it cannot establish which representation is better at a fixed weight. In a collaborator's fresh 100 grouped-split comparison at matched 25% weights, class-3 had lower mean MAE than alternate identity and won 94 splits. In that same experiment the 50% alternate-identity blend scored better than either 25% blend. Thus the evidence supports a modest matched-weight class-3 advantage at 25%, while the 50% alternate-identity model remains the best of these tested settings; representation and blend weight must not be conflated.

events.text: I’ll inspect the experiment and publication rules first, then choose a testable question and organize the work around it.
I’ll parallelize independent, held-out-testable prediction studies across the available scans while I inspect the datasets, baselines, and contribution schema.
I’ll inspect the experiment and publication requirements, then review the CASP3 data and available baselines to choose a defensible held-out prediction test.
I’ll inspect the experiment and publication workflow, then examine the KRAS datasets and available baselines to choose a reproducible prediction test.
I’ll inspect the experiment and publishing requirements, then review the BLAT datasets and available baselines before choosing a validation design.
I’ll inspect the experiment and publication workflow, then examine the KCNE1 data and identify a leakage-resistant held-out test.
I’ll check the experiment and publication workflow before inspecting CASP3 data and baselines.
I’ll inspect the full test schema and baseline implementation, then set up a reproducible validation study that can improve on the evaluator’s ridge baseline.
I’ll inspect both scans’ file formats, missingness, and baseline implementation so the validation metric and final held-out test match the evaluator’s setup.
I’ll inspect the KCNE1 score formats, dataset sizes, and available baselines before choosing a validation split and feature set.
I’ll inspect the CASP3 files and baseline definitions to understand available variants, labels, and the comparator before designing a leakage-safe validation split.
I’ll inspect both KRAS scan formats and their baseline predictors so I can design models that produce the evaluator’s required held-out `id,pred` files.
I’ll inspect the CASP3 files and baseline definitions to understand available variants, labels, and the comparator before designing a leakage-safe validation split.

Both datasets are single-substitution scans with enough observed variants for mutation-level validation. I’ll check the baseline and score distributions, then compare simple mutation/position encodings against the baseline using held-out training rows.
I’ll inspect the dataset documentation, table schema, and baseline implementation to determine the target and evaluator comparator.
The comparator is fixed-alpha one-hot ridge; I’ll test whether tuning its regularization improves held-out mutation prediction, while checking whether datasets can support cross-assay transfer.

I’m evaluating improvements over fixed alpha=1 one-hot ridge using mutation-level CV. Please report early validation results, artifact IDs and reusable code blobs on the board when ready; I’ll investigate cross-assay transfer and combined studies.
Both assays provide single-mutant sequences and scores, so I’ll check baseline definitions and mutation coverage to design consistent validation for expression and function.

The comparator is positional one-hot ridge, so I’ll check how mutation coverage is distributed and compare candidate models under random and position-held-out splits; this will show whether a simple improvement generalizes beyond familiar sites.

The two assays may offer complementary information: expression scores could help predict function even for variants held out from the function assay. I’ll quantify their overlap and relationship, and inspect how the evaluator baseline is implemented.

The scans assay the same protein under different conditions, so I’ll first benchmark tuned one-hot ridge against the fixed baseline with deterministic held-out splits, and assess whether cross-assay measurements help without using the target labels being predicted.

I’ll test a biologically informed extension to the ridge baseline: combine exact mutation-position features with amino-acid physicochemical descriptors, using validation to select model settings before held-out prediction.

I’ll benchmark the fixed ridge comparator against alpha-tuned positional encodings and a more strongly shared mutation-effect model, using repeated random splits and position-grouped splits to distinguish interpolation from site generalization.

I’ll test whether paired abundance and binding measurements can transfer information across assays. The key validation holds out variants from one assay while retaining their paired measurement in the other, and compares transfer models with the stated ridge baseline.

I’ll compare the fixed baseline with ridge regularization choices across reproducible random folds, and separately test whether the other BLAT scan’s score can transfer to variants withheld from the target scan.

Expression and function scores barely correlate across shared mutations, so I’ll model each assay separately. I’ll compare the evaluator’s one-hot ridge baseline with a physicochemical model under splits that hold out substitutions at represented sites.

The initial validation suggests that sharing mutation effects across sites may outperform positional ridge, but I’ll test a global wild-type→mutant substitution encoding across several random folds before selecting the final model.
I’ll test a cross-assay transfer hypothesis: where the same mutation appears in a paired scan, its measured score in that assay may improve prediction of the target assay beyond sequence-only ridge.

The first run exposed that the experiment environment sets `EVAL_DIR` even for validation runs, but has no held-out inputs there. I’ll inspect the execution environment and adjust mode detection before rerunning.
`EVAL_DIR` is present but empty during evidence runs, so the script mistakenly entered prediction mode. I’ll correct that check and run the planned within-site validation.

The paired-assay feature improves validation MAE over sequence-only ridge in both directions. I’ll verify the publication test requirements and harden prediction generation for variants lacking a paired public measurement before running held-out prediction tests.

The first validation favors the chemistry-informed ridge model on both assays under within-site mutation holdouts. I’ll inspect publication requirements and community work, then check whether site-held-out validation tells a different story before fixing the model for evaluation.

I’ll turn the best-performing, interpretable model into a reproducible script and validate it against the official ridge baseline on identical repeated folds; the script will also generate predictions from evaluator inputs.

The held-out variants likely share positions with the public set, but I’ll also test generalization to unseen positions to understand the model’s limits. I’ll inspect the artifact schema so the eventual prediction test runs with the right assay-specific model settings.

The two assays share most—but not all—variants, so I’ll test the paired-score feature with all training rows, explicitly marking missing cross-assay measurements. This better matches held-out evaluation and avoids restricting the model to only paired variants.
The reproducible CV run beats the fixed ridge comparator, so I’ll check the contribution schema and verify the saved script’s file handling before publishing a held-out prediction test.
Before publishing, I’ll confirm the prediction-test fields and command options so the evaluator can rerun the released code and score its predictions.

Across five random held-out splits, the paired-assay score plus sequence ridge improved MAE for both assays, including unpaired training variants. I’ll package the reproducible script and publish a held-out prediction test for each dataset.

I’ll add a stricter position-held-out check and make the released predictor robust to evaluator inputs that contain sequences but omit mutation labels. This will test whether the feature gains extend beyond substitutions at familiar sites.
The edit introduced literal escape characters in a dictionary, causing a syntax error before the validation could run. I’ll repair the formatting and rerun the experiment.
The inspection confirmed both the malformed line and that the earlier seed-count edit did not take effect. I’ll fix both before rerunning the position-held-out validation.
I’ll strengthen the evidence by adding position-held-out validation alongside repeated random folds, then rerun the released script so both metrics come from a recorded experiment.
I’ll publish one prediction contribution per assay, using the same reproducible model and reporting only validation metrics recorded by the five-split experiment.

Cross-assay calibration substantially outperformed the target-only ridge baseline on overlapping variants in the first validation. I’ll now test it more carefully with both random and residue-grouped folds, tune a blend against the target-only model, and build an evaluator-ready predictor with a fallback for variants missing from the companion scan.
The updated run failed because the position-held-out arrays were not initialized; I’ll inspect the script and correct the insertion before rerunning.
The group-split calculation is missing entirely; I’ll add it immediately before metrics are assembled and rerun to record valid metrics.
The abundance finding passed live checks. I’ll publish the reciprocal binding result, supported by the same validation experiment and paired-feature predictor.

The corrected run shows lower error for the mutation-feature ridge model on both random and position-held-out validation; I’ll package the final script and publish a hidden-set prediction test against the official baseline.
I’ll publish the reproducible prediction method with its recorded validation metrics and specify that the evaluator compares hidden-set MAE to the fixed one-hot ridge baseline.

Both prediction contributions passed live checks. I’ll explore whether simple nonlinear or position-specific transformations of the paired assay score improve validation further, and will only replace the published predictor if the evidence supports it.
The CASP3 finding is published; I’ll check whether other accepted work offers a method or result I can independently build on or test against this contribution.

Site-held-out scores show only modest gains from chemistry-informed features, while within-site validation favors them more strongly. I’ll test whether the other public KCNE1 assay adds useful, mutation-matched information without using held-out target scores.

The cross-assay signal remains strong even when target variants are grouped by residue, which reduces leakage from neighboring substitutions. I’ll verify the evaluator’s prediction-test format and inspect the complete fold results before locking the method and its fallback behavior.

Preliminary cross-assay validation is promising, especially for KRAS, but I’m correcting the evaluation pipeline so source-score imputation and scaling are learned only from each training fold and transferred unchanged to held-out variants.

The finding is published, and no other CASP3 work is available to extend. I’ll test whether adding site-specific alternate-residue effects improves on the published model under the same repeated held-out folds.

A stronger feature emerged: the paired-assay score interacted with mutation position, substantially reducing validation error in the grid search. I’ll assess ridge regularization for this position-specific transfer feature across the same five splits before updating the held-out predictor.

The cross-assay scores add little, so I’ll focus on the simpler chemistry-feature model. I’ll verify the evaluator path and make its prediction mode choose assay-specific regularization, then record a final evidence run.
Fold-held-out results show consistent gains from paired-assay scores, largest in KRAS; I’ll check for collaborators’ results before finalizing a reproducible held-out test.

Another researcher has independently established paired-assay transfer for KRAS; I’ll inspect their released methods and results, then extend the idea to the complementary KCNE1 scans rather than duplicate their KRAS claim.

The chemistry model consistently improves mutation-level holdout error over one-hot ridge, but gains are smaller for unseen positions. I’ll share this validation with the founder, then finalize the assay-specific held-out predictor.

The KRAS findings are accepted and independently align with my preliminary results; I’ll inspect their exact released implementation so I can test a genuine extension rather than duplicate their claim.

My first feature-interaction variants did not improve the published model, so I’ll test whether differential shrinkage of its existing feature groups can improve validation and, if successful, make a direct comparison against the published code.
I’ll build directly on the accepted KRAS transfer implementation, first verifying its released code and the execution interface so any extension genuinely consumes and improves on that work.
I’ll check the board command syntax and adapt the prediction script to identify the assay from evaluator-provided directories, with a fixed regularization value for each assay.

I’ll compare the accepted KRAS paired-score model against a fold-safe alternative, using the accepted code as an explicit input; this will let me test an extension on identical splits rather than claim a separate rediscovery.

I’ll make the predictor robust to either supported held-out directory layout and evaluate the exact fallback model against the fixed ridge baseline, using random and residue-grouped folds. At prediction time it will calibrate the companion assay only for mutations measured there and fall back to target-assay ridge otherwise.

Position-specific transfer improved validation further, with the lowest tested ridge penalty performing best in both assays. I’ll implement that predictor for evaluation, retain sequence-only fallback when the paired measurement is absent, and rerun the comparison using the exact released code.
I’ll share the initial results using the correct board syntax, then create a final predictor with assay-specific regularization and a confirmation split separate from the alpha-selection split.

KCNE1 early results: 10 repeated stratified within-position 20% mutation holdouts; chemistry-informed ridge (site intercept + pooled WT/alternate identity + six amino-acid property deltas, including position-specific deltas) reduced MAE vs baseline one-hot/ridge alpha=1. Expression: 0.15664 vs 0.20434 (best alpha 10); function: 0.17285 vs 0.19794 (best alpha 3). Grouped unseen-position MAE showed smaller gains: expression 0.27144 vs 0.27295; function 0.32745 vs 0.34927. Cross-assay scores added little. Final prediction code and fixed-alpha confirmation validation are in progress.

I’ll extend the accepted KRAS paired-assay approach to KCNE1 expression/function, explicitly reusing its released feature code and passing that work as an input; this tests whether the transfer finding generalizes to a new protein.
I’ll extend the accepted paired-assay feature method to KCNE1, consuming its shared feature implementation directly and testing transfer on held-out folds for the expression/function pair.

I’ll explore whether nonlinear similarity between substitutions improves on the published shared-effect ridge model, evaluating RBF kernel ridge on identical repeated folds and position-held-out folds.
The kernel experiment failed from an inconsistent substitution-feature offset; I’ll correct the offsets and rerun the same held-out comparison.

Position-specific transfer substantially outperformed the earlier paired-score model in both assays across all five validation splits. I’ll package this predictor and publish updated held-out tests, with the new experiment as evidence.
The accepted KRAS method exposes reusable encoding and paired-feature functions; I’ll verify how its code blob is mounted in an evidence run before using those functions in the KCNE1 extension.
This run hit an unsupported `dense_output` argument; I’ll remove it and rerun the kernel comparison.
One configuration still had too-small matrix dimensions for its appended residue features; I’ll inspect the feature ranges and correct each total dimension before rerunning.
The position-specific model is validated and packaged. I’ll publish updated held-out prediction tests for abundance and binding, reporting the five-split MAEs from the recorded run.
The wild-type and alternate-residue feature offsets overlapped the dimension boundary; I’ll place them in their intended non-overlapping ranges and rerun the experiment.
The updated abundance test passed live checks. I’ll publish the parallel DARPin K55 binding result using the same position-specific transfer model and recorded validation evidence.

I’ve confirmed the collaborator’s released code arrives as an archive; I’ll import its one-hot and paired-feature functions in the experiment, then measure whether paired KCNE1 scores improve both assays over the baseline.
I’ll make the prediction test work for either assay without relying on an implicit assay default, and run a fresh, fixed-hyperparameter validation on new within-position holdouts.
Both position-specific predictions are published. I’ll check for other researchers’ accepted KRAS work so I can identify a concrete opportunity to replicate, extend, or correct an independent result.

Paired-assay transfer generalized only weakly to KCNE1 in my validation, so I won’t overstate it; I’ll check collaborators’ other accepted results for a stronger opportunity to extend or rigorously challenge their findings.

The independent fixed-alpha confirmation split preserves the improvement for both assays. I’ll package the final prediction code, verify the required test fields, and report the recorded evidence to the founder.

KCNE1 fixed-alpha confirmation evidence exec-51100d72: on 10 fresh 20%-per-site mutation holdout splits, chemistry ridge beats one-hot ridge in both assays. Expression MAE 0.15946 vs 0.20522 (alpha 10; mean improvement 0.04577); function MAE 0.17596 vs 0.20280 (alpha 3; improvement 0.02684). Final self-contained code is ready for held-out prediction tests.

A collaborator reports strong KCNE1 gains from chemistry-informed features, while KRAS position-specific transfer is also emerging; I’ll inspect those accepted contributions and target a rigorous extension with clear added value.

The community has an independent CASP3 mutation-effect result. I’ll inspect its claim and method, then test whether its shared mutation-effect approach adds evidence or a useful comparison for the KRAS scans.

The accepted CASP3 study found that sharing substitution effects helps even at unseen positions; I’ll test whether that insight transfers to BLAT, using its released code as an input and validating against fixed positional one-hot ridge.

The fixed-alpha validation is recorded, and the packaged code is stored. I’ll publish separate held-out prediction findings for expression and function so each is evaluated on its own assay and baseline.

The stronger position-specific predictor is published. I’ll share the validated KRAS results with the founder, then test whether adding mutation-identity interactions gives further gains beyond the position-specific feature.

KRAS results: paired cross-assay DMS score with a mutation-position interaction plus one-hot sequence improved five-split MAE vs alpha=1 sequence ridge. Abundance: 0.21277 -> 0.15976; DARPin K55: 0.14897 -> 0.11395. Prediction artifacts findin-4960c9e8 / findin-57ff7d58; reusable code blob 4e2338514e7283487d22e085c86c2a44600d4b37fc3033b2f4cf7962c275ebaa. Validated in exec-eb82d564.
Both findings passed live checks, and each includes an assay-specific held-out prediction test. I’ll share the artifact IDs and reusable code with the founder.

Published KCNE1 prediction findings: expression findin-10a364a4; function findin-d3bcf6f7. Reusable predictor code blob: 9bf4995beb17ad6c0d7b6d3da37aa78965c7c91cbfd01b53d53c9dbaf74865db. Fixed-alpha confirmation evidence: exec-51100d72. Both publication live checks passed.

Exact cross-assay transfer is compelling only when the companion scan has measurements for evaluator inputs. To avoid overstating that result, I’ll validate an additional setting where companion measurements for each held-out target variant are masked and must be predicted from the remaining companion data.

To build materially on the accepted CASP3 result, I’ll inspect its released mutation-effect encoding and test whether shared substitution features improve KRAS transfer predictions beyond my position-specific model.
I’ve retrieved the CASP3 model artifact. I’ll inspect its code to reproduce the shared mutation-effect features faithfully before comparing them on KRAS.
The artifact downloaded as a single file rather than an unpacked directory. I’ll inspect its archive contents and read the model script.
The downloaded code blob is not a ZIP archive. I’ll identify its format and extract or inspect the bundled files so the KRAS comparison can faithfully reuse the CASP3 encoding.
The code blob is a tar archive. I’ll extract the released script and inspect its feature construction.

The findings are published and shared. Before wrapping up, I’ll smoke-test both assay-specific prediction paths using unlabeled synthetic variant inputs, checking that the released script writes valid `id,pred` files in evaluator mode.

The CASP3 result suggests shared substitution effects can generalize to unseen sites; I’ll test that mechanism on both BLAT scans, using the accepted CASP3 code as an input and checking random and position-held-out validation.
The released predictor passes a smoke test for both assays. I’ll check for new community results and compare validation models to see whether a materially stronger approach is worth contributing.

Shared substitution features improve both BLAT scans in random and unseen-position validation, extending the accepted CASP3 method to a new protein and two assays; I’ll package the reproducible predictor and publish separate held-out tests for each scan.

I’ve completed the KCNE1 findings. To look for a concrete collaboration opportunity, I’ll inspect the accepted shared-mutation modeling result and determine whether its method can be tested on KCNE1 rather than merely cited.

The CASP3 finding uses shared wild-type-to-alternate mutation features, a plausible extension to my KCNE1 model. I’ll retrieve its released code and test whether adding that feature materially improves KCNE1 validation.
The released CASP3 code was fetched as a single file. I’ll inspect its feature construction so I can reproduce the shared-substitution idea in the KCNE1 validation without changing the comparator.
The fetched code is a tar archive rather than a plain Python file. I’ll extract it and inspect the shared-substitution features before implementing the KCNE1 extension.

The kernel alternatives did not beat the published model consistently; I’ll smoke-test the released prediction script with an evaluator-shaped input file to verify it writes the required `id,pred` output.

The accepted CASP3 method adds explicit wild-type→alternate substitution indicators. I’ll extend my KCNE1 chemistry model with those 400 pair features and compare the extension against both chemistry-only ridge and one-hot ridge on the same mutation-level holdouts.

The CASP3 model uses reusable shared mutation features: position, wild-type residue, alternate residue, and wild-type→alternate pair. I’ll import that published feature encoder through its code blob and test whether it adds value to the KRAS position-transfer model.

The shared-effect model beats positional ridge on both BLAT assays, including held-out mutation positions; I’ll publish separate reproducible predictions for each dataset and explicitly record that the work extends the accepted CASP3 method.
The smoke test’s login shell failed before running the script; I’ll rerun it without a login shell and check that the evaluator-style predictions are recorded.
Both BLAT contributions passed live checks; I’ll review the full community’s accepted work and incoming results to identify another useful extension or correction.

The KCNE1 chemistry-informed findings are accepted; I’ll examine their released model and validation design to test a substantive extension—whether chemistry features add value over shared substitution effects, especially at unseen positions.

KCNE1’s accepted model uses physicochemical substitution features, while CASP3’s accepted model shares categorical mutation effects; I’ll test whether combining them improves KCNE1 prediction beyond chemistry alone, especially when entire sites are held out.
The evaluator-shaped prediction run successfully produced `predictions.csv`; I’ll notify the founder of the published artifact, reproducible code blob, and evidence run.
The CASP3 prediction test produced the required output; I’ll report the published finding and its code and evidence IDs to the founder.

CASP3 brief complete: published findin-396aafc2, 'Shared mutation-effect ridge improves CASP3 activity prediction.' Reproducible code blob: 69f2a974fc36a39c21a5d5bf7c430776b26d5600ab9a3a74875e7695b990ce00. Successful evidence: exec-0723d48a (random CV MAE 0.44319 vs baseline 0.48955; position-held-out MAE 0.54457 vs 0.58046). Prediction output smoke-tested in exec-ce5ee7bf.

The published CASP3 shared-mutation encoding did not improve the KRAS position-transfer model in validation; combining them worsened MAE in both assays. I’ll run a clean five-split comparison with the shared encoder loaded from the CASP3 code blob, then prepare held-out comparisons that directly test this extension.
I’ll smoke-test the held-out prediction path against a small fixture, then remove the fixture so the released code blob contains only reproducible predictor code.

I’ll test whether adding CASP3’s shared wild-type→alternate substitution feature to the accepted KCNE1 chemistry model improves prediction, especially for entirely unseen sites; I’ll consume both accepted code blobs and compare against chemistry alone and the official ridge baseline.

I’ll extend the accepted CASP3 shared-mutation encoding to KCNE1, combining its explicit WT→alternate pair features with my physicochemical features. I’ll load the published feature implementation through the experiment input, and compare both models on paired tuning and confirmation splits.

I’ll test whether a lightly regularized site-by-alternate-residue interaction adds predictive value beyond the published shared-mutation model, using the same repeated folds and a position-held-out check.
